description_full: Brady Corporation manufactures and supplies identification solutions and workplace safety products that identify and protect premises, products, and people in the Americas, Asia, Europe, and Australia. The company offers safety signs, traffic signs and control products, floor-marking tapes, pipe markers, labeling systems, spill control products, lockout/tagout devices, personal protection equipment, first aid products, and software and services for safety compliance auditing, procedures writing, and training; materials, radio frequency identification and barcode scanners for product identification, direct part marking, engraving equipment, brand protection labeling, work in process labeling, finished product identification, asset tracking labels, asset tags, and industrial track and trace applications; and handheld printers, wire markers, sleeves, and tags. It also provides wristbands, labels, printing systems, and other products used in hospital, laboratory, and other healthcare settings for tracking and improving the safety of patients; and name tags, badges, lanyards, rigid card printing systems, and access control software. The company serves industrial manufacturing, electronic manufacturing, healthcare, chemical, oil, gas, alternative energy, automotive, aerospace, governments, mass transit, mechanical contractors, construction, utilities, education, leisure and entertainment, retail and telecommunications, and others. The company markets and sells its products through multiple channels, including distributors, a direct sales force, and digital channels. Brady Corporation was incorporated in 1914 and is based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
ceo_bio: Mr. Vineet A. Nargolwala | President, CEO & Director | Age 52 | Compensation: $641,576 (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 6K people. Revenue per employee of $263K ranks in the bottom quartile among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $30K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Brady Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.7B market cap on $1.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 8% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 50%.

The business throws off $193M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.19× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 27× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 2.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.7% of the shares.

Industrials ETF trading well below its long-term trend

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 7pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.44x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 15% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 19% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.71, it is more defensive than the market.
About $19.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 23% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 9% below its DCF fair value of $86.25, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $69.88 to $110 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 18.3 vs 23.3 and EV/EBITDA 10.6 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 8% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $110 on average, 40% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 8.3% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.74).
It runs a 50% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.19x.
ROE of 15% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.7% of revenue on R&D and 1.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $172.2M (5% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.2, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.7% over 3 years, 7.7% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 23% of profits supports about 4.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 3.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.6% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.7%, and institutions hold 88%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year, net $385K bought.
It returns 2.4% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 33 consecutive years.
people: With about 6,325 employees, each generates about $263K of revenue, 0.7x the Industrials median.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $642K (2x revenue per employee).
